Regression for network data

Source: R/model_regression.R
regression.Rd

Fits a regression model to one (or a list of) manynet-compatible network(s) using the multiple regression quadratic assignment procedure (MRQAP).

The formula front end is the familiar y ~ ego(attr) + alter(attr) + same(attr) + diff(attr) syntax, plus terms computed on other layers of the network, such as recip(friends), and plain references to those layers. Its terms follow {goldfish}'s where the two packages share them. Internally the response and predictors are packed into matrices and handed to a QAP engine (ported from MrQAP) that supports:

  • gaussian, binomial, poisson, negative binomial, and zero-inflated Poisson families;

  • two permutation schemes: "predictor" (Dekker's double semi-partialling) and "outcome";

  • random intercepts (lme4), and fixed effects, absorbed as in {fixest};

  • robust (HC3) standard errors;

  • lists of networks, in which graphs that are missing any predictor are dropped with a warning and the remaining networks are pooled;

  • cognitive social structures, detected rather than declared (see below).

Usage

estimate_mrqap(formula, .data, times = 1000, control = list())

net_regression(formula, .data, times = 1000, control = list())

Arguments

formula

A formula describing the model. The left-hand side is the dependent network: a layer, a tie attribute such as weight, or . for the network's focal layer or the whole network. The right-hand side accepts these terms, whose arguments can be given by position or by name:

  • ego(attr, levels = NULL), alter(attr, levels = NULL) — the sender's or the receiver's value of a node attribute; a categorical attribute is dummy-coded, with the first category as the reference,

  • same(attr, diff = FALSE, levels = NULL) — 1 where sender and receiver share an attribute value; with diff = TRUE, as in ergm's nodematch(), one 0/1 column for each category, 1 where sender and receiver both hold it. match(attr) is a deprecated alias of same(attr, diff = TRUE),

  • diff(attr, transformer_fn = abs) — the transformed difference between the sender's and the receiver's values: absolute by default, and signed with transformer_fn = identity. dist(attr) is a deprecated alias,

  • sim(attr) — proportional similarity in a numeric attribute, 1 - |d| / range,

  • mix(attr, levels = NULL) — one 0/1 column for each pair of a sender's and a receiver's category, less the first pair as the reference. The pairs are in ergm's order for nodemix(), the sender's category changing fastest,

  • tie(layer, weighted = FALSE) — another layer as a dyadic covariate, 0/1 unless weighted = TRUE; a layer or tie attribute named on its own enters with its values as stored,

  • exchange(layer) — the reverse tie, j to i, in another layer; recip(layer) is the same, and recip(), or recip on its own, reads the outcome's own reverse tie, and warns,

  • indeg(layer, type = "alter", weighted = FALSE) and outdeg(layer, type = "alter", weighted = FALSE) — a node's number of incoming or outgoing ties in another layer, for the receiver ("alter") or the sender ("ego"),

  • tertius(layer, attr, summarizer_fn = "mean") — the mean (or the tie-weighted sum, with "sum") of an attribute over the receiver's in-neighbours in a layer, other than the sender. A receiver with no other in-neighbour takes the mean of the defined cells. The older tertius(attr) reads the outcome's own ties, and warns,

  • tertius_diff(layer, attr, summarizer_fn = "mean") — how far the sender's value lies from that mean, as an absolute difference,

  • global(var) — a network-level variable from the network's globals, in a list of networks; on one network it is the intercept.

: and * give interactions of any order, as the product of the terms.

levels = chooses the categories that get a column in ego(), alter(), and same(), or the pairs in mix(), as in ergm. Give the names, such as levels = c("sales", "hr") or, for mix(), levels = "sales -> hr", written as in fit$terms (-- for an undirected network). Or give positions in the order of the columns, where a negative position leaves that one out: levels = -1 is the default of ego(), alter(), and mix(). In ego(), alter(), and mix(), the categories left out are the reference together; where every one is chosen, the first chosen is the reference. In same(), a dyad that shares a category left out is not counted. An unknown name aborts and lists the categories. A term with more than ten categories and no levels = warns, since under permute = "predictor" each column is permuted on its own.

A formula written for {goldfish} or {ergm} can be used as it is. It is first read by specify_mrqap(), which rewrites each term that has an MRQAP equivalent, such as ergm's nodematch("dept") as same(dept), and drops each term that an MRQAP cannot fit, such as goldfish's inertia or ergm's gwesp(), which read the outcome's own ties. One warning names each dropped term and the reason, and the rest of the model is fitted. A name that no model knows aborts and suggests the nearest term, as does a formula with no term left to fit.

A bar adds a random intercept, as in {lme4}: (1 | sender), (1 | receiver), (1 | reporter) for a cognitive social structure, or (1 | network) for a list of networks. Each sets the same switch as its random_intercept_* control. Random slopes are not supported.

A bar outside parentheses absorbs fixed effects, as in {fixest}: y ~ x | sender + receiver (see the section on fixed effects).

.data

A manynet-consistent network (see manynet::as_tidygraph()), or a list of such networks. When a list is supplied the model is fit jointly; graphs missing any predictor are dropped with a warning.

times

Integer. Number of permutations for the null distribution. 1000 is the default; publication-ready work usually needs 1000-10000.

control

The controls of the model, as the result of control_mrqap() or a named list of its arguments, such as list(family = "poisson", seed = 1). A control that is not named keeps its default. See control_mrqap() for each control, its default, and the names it converts from other models and earlier versions.

Value

An object of class netreg, with a more specific class in front: netreg_lm for a gaussian model and netreg_glm for any other family. A cognitive social structure also puts netreg_css first, so c("netreg_css", "netreg_glm", "netreg") for a binomial CSS model. A method can be written for any of these, and falls back to the next. Among its elements:

  • coefficients and obs, the estimates and the observed test statistics of the model;

  • lower, larger, and abs, the share of permutations whose coefficient (first row) or test statistic (second row) is at or below, at or above, or beyond the observed one;

  • testdist, the permuted test statistics themselves, as a matrix of one row per permutation and one column per coefficient. The shares in lower, larger, and abs are read from it. Under permute = "predictor" each column comes from its own set of permutations, so rows pair columns only by position, and the intercept column is NA. A permutation that failed leaves its row NA.

  • panel, whether the network was fitted as a panel of its waves.

  • missing, a list of the treatment of unobserved dyads, the number of dyads the model could use (possible) and did use (used), the number unobserved on each variable (unobserved), the number of fixed ties left out (fixed_ties), and the number of nodes that stayed in place in each permutation set (fixed_nodes).

  • fixed_effects, the groups whose fixed effects were absorbed;

  • pred, the dyad-level data, with the observed values even where a gaussian model was fitted to demeaned ones;

  • terms, a tibble of one row for each coefficient, with the parts that its name joins: term, the coefficient's name; effect, the formula term it comes from, such as "ego" or "same", or "intercept" or "interaction"; its layer and attribute; its category and the reference category it is compared with, where the term is categorical; and for an interaction, its operands, the names of the columns it multiplies. tidy() adds these columns to the estimates.

When the outcome is binary – either family = "binomial" or "gaussian" with a 0/1 dependent – a probabilistic confusion matrix is attached as $confusion_matrix; for the gaussian-binary case the linear probability fitted values are clamped to 0/1 before sampling.

Functions

  • net_regression(): The name this function had in {migraph}, and in infernet before 0.4.0. It still works, and warns once that it is deprecated.

Cognitive social structures

A cognitive social structure (CSS) records each person's report of the whole network (Krackhardt 1987). {manynet} holds one as a network whose ties carry a by column naming the reporter, and manynet::is_cognitive() says whether a network is one. Where the outcome is a CSS, the model is fitted on every reported dyad: one observation for each sender, receiver, and reporter, rather than for each sender and receiver.

  • A nodal term such as ego(age) is the same in every report.

  • A layer that is itself a CSS, such as another relation that every reporter described, enters as each reporter's own report of it.

  • A layer that is not a CSS, such as a formal reporting structure, enters as one matrix that every report shares.

  • tertius(), recip(), indeg(), and outdeg() on a CSS layer are computed within each report, since each reporter sees different ties.

A permutation relabels the nodes, and a reporter is a node, so the senders, receivers, and reporters are relabelled together. (1 | reporter) in the formula adds a random intercept for each reporter.

A person who was not asked has a report of zeros unless the network marks them as missing, for example with manynet::mutate_nodes(net, na = label %in% c(...)). Their reports are then dropped. A report of zeros that is not so marked is kept, and named in a warning, since it may be either.

Missing data

An unobserved dyad is an NA in the outcome or in a predictor, never a zero tie. {manynet} records unobserved ties, and a CSS reporter who was not asked, and manynet::as_matrix() turns both into NA. By default (control = list(missing = "available")), the model drops each unobserved dyad and says how many it dropped on each variable.

A permutation must then be fitted on the same dyads as the observed model, or the null distribution rests on more data than the estimate it is compared with. So nodes are permuted only among nodes with the same unobserved cells: a node that did not report, a node that nobody reported on, a reporter who was not asked, and a fully observed node are each exchanged only with nodes of their own kind. A node with scattered unobserved cells stays in place. This restricts the null hypothesis to exchangeability within those blocks, and with many fixed nodes it leaves few distinct permutations, which is reported with a warning.

control = list(missing = "fail") stops instead, for a user who wants no dyad dropped without their decision. Multiple imputation is not yet available.

A tie that {manynet} marks as fixed, in its fixed tie column, was set by the design rather than chosen, so it is no observation of the process. It is left out of the model, counted apart from the unobserved dyads, and kept in place under permutation, as an unobserved dyad is. "fail" does not stop on it.

A cell that cannot hold a tie, such as a tie between two levels of a multilevel network that the design rules out, is a structural zero rather than missing data. {manynet} does not yet mark such cells, so they enter the model as observed zeros. Remove them, or set them to NA, before fitting.

Longitudinal networks

A longitudinal network, one that manynet::is_longitudinal() says has more than one wave, is fitted as a panel. Each wave but the first is an outcome, and the waves are pooled, so the network index is the wave. One permutation relabels the nodes the same way in every wave, so that each node keeps its own trajectory under the null hypothesis.

Three of goldfish's effects then read the outcome's previous wave, as goldfish and RSiena read the state of the network before each change:

  • inertia, the tie from i to j in the previous wave;

  • recip, the tie from j to i in the previous wave;

  • trans, the number of two-paths i -> k -> j in the previous wave, counting only observed ties.

On a cross-sectional network, inertia and trans are dropped with a warning, since they could only read the outcome's own ties, and recip reads the outcome's reverse tie, with a warning. Every other term, including a layer such as tie(friends) and a node attribute, reads the same wave as the outcome; see stocnet/infernet#18. Every wave must hold the same nodes: mark a node that is absent from a wave as missing there. A list of networks is read as independent networks, not as a panel, even where it holds the waves of one network.

Fixed effects

A bar outside parentheses absorbs a fixed effect for each group named after it, as in {fixest}: weight ~ sim(age) | sender + receiver. The groups are sender, receiver, reporter for a cognitive social structure, and network for a list of networks. In a pooled list each node's group is within its own network; in a panel a node keeps one group across the waves, and network is one effect for each wave. The intercept is one of the absorbed effects, so its estimate is NA.

A gaussian model is demeaned once by the fixed effects, and each permutation fits a plain model of the demeaned variables. A node permutation maps senders onto senders and receivers onto receivers, and every permutation fits the dyads of the observed model, so this gives the same estimates as a dummy for every group (the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem), at the cost of a model without them. Its R-squared is the within R-squared. Any other family is fitted with fixest::feglm(), or fixest::fenegbin() for "negbin", in every permutation, which needs {fixest}. That leaves out the dyads of a group whose outcome has one value, and says how many.

A predictor that does not vary within the groups, such as ego(age) with a sender effect, is absorbed by them, and aborts with its name. An undirected network has no senders or receivers, so it drops those effects with a warning, as it does those random intercepts. A two-mode network keeps both, since its rows and columns are different nodes. Fixed effects cannot yet be combined with random intercepts, robust standard errors, or the "zip" family.

Multiplex networks

The left-hand side of the formula can name a layer of a multiplex network, and the right-hand side can name other layers as dyadic covariates, e.g. advice ~ friends + reports on manynet::ison_hightech. A network that declares a focal layer, as info$focal, takes it as the outcome of . ~, and says so. A named left-hand side takes priority. A multiplex network whose layers cannot be combined into one matrix, such as one with a CSS layer, must name its outcome layer or declare one.

A term built from a layer must not read the outcome's own ties, since permuting the outcome does not permute such a predictor with it. tie(), indeg(), and outdeg() refuse the outcome layer. recip(), tertius(), and tertius_diff() without a layer read the outcome, and warn.

References

Krackhardt, David. 1987. "Cognitive Social Structures." Social Networks 9(2): 109-134. doi:10.1016/0378-8733(87)90009-8 .

Krackhardt, David. 1988. "Predicting with Networks: Nonparametric Multiple Regression Analysis of Dyadic Data." Social Networks 10(4):359-81. doi:10.1016/0378-8733(88)90004-4 .

Haunss, Sebastian, and James Hollway. 2023. "Multimodal mechanisms of political discourse dynamics and the case of Germany's nuclear energy phase-out." Network Science 11(2): 205-223. doi:10.1017/nws.2022.31 .

Dekker, David, David Krackhardt, and Tom A. B. Snijders. 2007. "Sensitivity of MRQAP tests to collinearity and autocorrelation conditions." Psychometrika 72(4): 563-581. doi:10.1007/s11336-007-9016-1 .

See also

Other models: control_mrqap(), print.netreg_lm(), specify, tests

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
networkers <- manynet::ison_networkers |>
  manynet::to_subgraph(Discipline == "Sociology")
model1 <- estimate_mrqap(
  weight ~ ego(Citations) + alter(Citations) + sim(Citations),
  networkers, times = 20)
print(model1)
} # }
# A cognitive social structure: each of 21 managers' report of who goes to
# whom for advice, against the formal reporting structure that all share.
css_model <- estimate_mrqap(advice ~ same(dept) + reports,
                            manynet::ison_hightech, times = 5)
